title: 25. Behavioral, Work Experience Survey & EPIC
description: Turing's 57-question Work Experience Survey (ethics/situational MCQ that gates access to later stages) + 8-slot STAR bank + Andela EPIC-mapped stories + communication drills.

25.1 Turing Work Experience Survey (57 Q: Answer HONESTLY — Turing cross-checks against later interview responses
There's no 'right' answer — pattern of choices is scored
Topics: professional ethics, feedback reception, bug handling, code quality standards, team collaboration, self-improvement, work-under-pressure
Failing to complete = failing to unlock later stages
25.3 Andela EPIC (2-3 stories per value): Excellence — attention to detail, thoroughness under time pressure
Passion — genuine enthusiasm shown through action
Integrity — honesty about capability, delivering on commitments
25.4 Communication Drills: Written status update — clear, scannable, action-oriented
Difficult message delivery — deadline slip, downgrade, disagreement

questions.prompt: You discover a production bug that causes minor UI glitch for 1% of users. Your PM says 'ignore it, we ship the new feature Friday.' You:

options.text: Log the bug in the tracker + estimate fix time; if <2 hours, offer to include in Friday; if larger, agree to defer + set follow-up date

questions.explanation: Ethics: log + estimate + offer trade — professional response. Silent fixes are unauditable. Public pushback burns political capital unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: You're asked to ship a feature 'quick and dirty' due to a deadline. Best approach?

options.text: Ship the thinnest working slice, document the shortcuts explicitly, create follow-up tickets to repay debt within a defined window

questions.explanation: Deliberate tech debt is fine; hidden tech debt isn't. Naming shortcuts publicly makes them repayable.

questions.prompt: A senior engineer leaves 15 comments on your PR, several sharply critical. You:

options.text: Thank them, address each comment (fix or explain rationale), close-out with a summary

questions.explanation: Feedback is signal. Handle each — either fix or explain. Manager escalation is for personal-attack territory, not code review.

questions.prompt: You disagree with your team's technical direction. Most productive next step:

options.text: Write up your case in a doc, share it, propose a decision meeting; commit fully to whatever's decided
Go around the team to leadership

questions.explanation: Disagree and commit. Written case beats verbal debate. Escalation is for principled disagreement (ethics, safety), not preference.

questions.prompt: A production incident happened during your on-call. Root cause is a config change from a different team. Your response after resolution:

options.text: Write the post-mortem, name the config change as the trigger without blame, propose a process fix (better staging validation) that would have caught it

questions.explanation: Blameless post-mortem. Focus on systemic fix. Ownership is naming root cause without finger-pointing.

questions.prompt: You realize you've been coasting on skills you learned 3 years ago. Best action:

options.text: Wait for a project to force you
Pick 1 concrete skill gap, define a 90-day goal + weekly practice, integrate it into a real project

questions.explanation: Focused skill acquisition beats broad course-hopping. Integration with real work = retention.

questions.prompt: PM asks 'how long for feature X?' You've never built anything like it. Best response:

options.text: Guess a small number to look confident
'I need 2 hours to spike + break it down. Then I can give a real estimate.'

questions.explanation: Fake precision is worse than 'I don't know yet.' Spike + estimate is the professional response.

questions.prompt: Customer asks you to disable audit logging on a specific report. It's compliance-relevant. You:

options.text: Explain the compliance implication + offer alternative (log filtering, cleaner UI); if they insist, escalate to your legal/compliance

questions.explanation: The customer isn't always right when compliance is on the line. Explain, offer alternative, escalate if needed. Silent compliance-bypass is fireable.

questions.prompt: You realize Wednesday you'll miss Friday's deadline. Best next step:

options.text: Tell stakeholders immediately with revised estimate + trade-off options (cut scope vs extend)

questions.explanation: Early bad news is cheaper than late bad news. Options empower decision-makers.

questions.prompt: You're assigned a ticket with unclear acceptance criteria. First step:

options.text: Interpret and implement your best guess
Comment on ticket with 2-3 specific clarification questions before starting
Ask the whole team in standup

questions.explanation: Specific clarification questions unblock without wasted work. Standup blocks 6 people for one person's problem.

questions.prompt: Reviewing a colleague's PR that works but is hard to read. You:

options.text: Approve with note: 'works, but here are 2 refactor suggestions for a follow-up PR — don't want to block shipping'

questions.explanation: Ship + suggest. Don't gatekeep on preference. Reject only for correctness or security.

questions.prompt: You notice a teammate is showing signs of burnout. Best action:

options.text: Private 1:1 to check in, no advice unless asked; if serious, encourage them to talk to their manager

questions.explanation: Care without violating trust. Their manager conversation is their choice, not yours to make.

questions.prompt: Two managers give you conflicting priorities. Best action:

options.text: Get both in a 15-min call to align. Don't let them use you as a proxy for their disagreement.

questions.explanation: Force the alignment upstream. Being a proxy is a losing pattern.

questions.prompt: Your work is presented at a company all-hands but only your manager's name is mentioned. Response:

options.text: 1:1 with your manager afterward — 'I noticed my name wasn't mentioned; going forward, I'd appreciate credit on public presentations. Anything I should do differently to make that natural?'

questions.explanation: Direct, private, low-drama conversation. Assumes good intent. Asks for what you want.

questions.prompt: You accidentally discover a security vulnerability in a system you don't own. You:

options.text: Report privately to the owning team + security team; don't disclose publicly until patched
Post in company Slack for visibility

questions.explanation: Responsible disclosure applies internally too. Public Slack alerts attackers. Silent fix isn't audited.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a project you owned end-to-end. 60-90 sec.

rubric.criterion: T: clear task with YOUR ownership scope
R: measurable result with a number

questions.modelAnswer: S: Onboarding funnel dropped 40% at step 3. T: I owned reducing that. A: Session-replay analysis found 3 friction points; prototyped fixes in a week; A/B tested one at a time; shipped the winner. R: 40% → 18% drop-off in 6 weeks, ~$300k ARR added. Reflection: session replays are now my first move on any funnel problem.

questions.prompt: Describe a time you handled a difficult stakeholder.
questions.modelAnswer: S: PM kept escalating we were unresponsive. T: I owned turning it around in a quarter. A: 1:1 to understand — turned out they needed predictability, not speed. Introduced weekly written status + decision log. R: Zero escalations that quarter; format adopted by 2 other teams.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a technical decision you reversed.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Chose Kafka for a low-throughput event bus. T: Two months in, usage 10 events/sec, ops burden disproportionate. A: Proposed SQS, migrated writers behind feature flag, drained Kafka, decommissioned. R: 60% infra cost drop; on-call load fell. Learned to insist on 90-day cost/ops review on default infra picks.

questions.prompt: Cross-team alignment without formal authority — example?
questions.modelAnswer: S: Three teams owned pieces of billing pipeline with incompatible retry semantics. T: I wanted single strategy but couldn't mandate. A: Wrote 2-page proposal, ran review with all three leads; agreed on shared idempotency key + backoff library. R: End-to-end retry bugs from ~5/month → 0 for two quarters. Written proposal beat meetings.

questions.prompt: Shipping under tight deadline with imperfect info.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Investor demo in 5 days with broken data pipeline. T: I owned credible end-to-end story. A: Scoped demo to 2 clean accounts; documented shortcut; ran pipeline nightly (not real-time) for demo; told lead + CEO explicitly what shipped. R: Demo landed the round; filled in real-time piece next sprint. Naming shortcuts publicly makes them repayable.

questions.prompt: Describe a project or deployment that failed.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Led a migration that took API down 40 min. T: I owned cutover. A: Had rollback but hadn't rehearsed it; when we needed it, rollback also failed. Recovered by manually reverting DNS. R: 40-min outage. Since then, every migration rehearses rollback in staging first. Last PG16 migration used the rehearsed rollback cleanly — 3-min hiccup instead of 40.

questions.prompt: Describe a pattern you spotted across multiple projects.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Across five customers deploying our webhook integration, same failure at month 2 — their receiver started dropping traffic under load. T: I owned pattern reports to product. A: Documented with logs from all five, proposed opt-in client-side rate-limiter library. R: Shipped in v2.3; new customers stopped hitting the failure. FDEs are earliest signal source for product.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you told a customer no and held the line.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Customer asked to disable audit logging on a specific report because noisy. T: I owned the answer. A: Acknowledged the pain — noise hides signals — but disabling audit was compliance risk to their regulator. Offered log filtering + cleaner UI. R: They accepted; their compliance team later thanked me directly when the regulator asked for that log.

questions.prompt: Why FDE and not regular SWE?

rubric.criterion: Connects to specific past customer-facing work

questions.modelAnswer: Last three years, either sitting with customers or building for internal teams with the same feedback loop. What I like: problems start messy — real data, real politics, real deadlines — and you end with something that actually works in their environment, not just mine. FDE makes that the whole job. Looking at [company] because [specific real reason tied to their work].

questions.prompt: Why this company specifically?

rubric.criterion: Cites actual customers / products / research (not generic)

questions.modelAnswer: Two specific reasons. First, [product / customer you actually admire] — I read their [engineering blog post / paper / release]; the [specific detail] mapped to problems I've hit. Second, the FDE-track focus on [industry/vertical] fits my [background element]. I want to work close to customers on hard integration problems, and this role literally is that.

questions.prompt: Tell me about operating in an unfamiliar environment.

rubric.criterion: Shows ramp-up: who you talked to, what you read, how you tested understanding
How you shipped value while still learning

questions.modelAnswer: S: Joined a project where the codebase was in a language I hadn't shipped before + the customer domain was finance-specific. T: I owned an integration by week 3. A: Week 1: shadowed 3 engineers, read the top 5 files in the repo, ran the app locally to trace one flow end-to-end. Week 2: took a small ticket to learn the workflow. Week 3: owned the integration. R: Shipped on time, no major bugs. Learned that the fastest ramp-up is trace one end-to-end flow in production before touching code.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Excellence: tell me about attention to detail under time pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Rushing to ship a payment migration, tempted to skip the reconciliation report. T: I owned the migration. A: Insisted on running the reconciliation even though 4 hours behind schedule — caught 3 mismatched transactions that would have led to double-charged customers. R: Fixed before deploy. Zero customer complaints. Would have been a P0 incident had we shipped.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Excellence: a time you went beyond 'done' to 'done well'.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Task was 'add a new API endpoint'. T: I owned it. A: 'Done' would have been the endpoint + one test. I added: input validation with Zod, per-endpoint rate limit, integration test covering 3 edge cases, and updated the OpenAPI spec + client SDK. R: When a customer hit an edge case a month later, our error message + docs meant they self-served the fix without a support ticket. Small extra effort, real ongoing value.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Passion: something you built or learned outside required work.

rubric.criterion: Why it mattered to YOU specifically

questions.modelAnswer: S: Was curious about how LLMs handle long context. T: Self-directed. A: Spent 3 weekends building a mini RAG system over my own notes; wrote it up on GitHub with tests. R: Now I use RAG patterns confidently at work — including the failure modes I discovered (chunk boundaries dropping context, cheap embeddings underperforming). Learned by shipping is faster than learning by reading.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Passion: how do you keep up with the field?

rubric.criterion: How you filter signal from noise
Example of applying something you learned

questions.modelAnswer: Weekly ritual: Monday morning skim Hacker News + one deep-dive paper from Anthropic/OpenAI research. Follow 4 specific engineers on Twitter for signal. Build one small thing per month using something new — that's how it sticks. Recent example: read about MCP, built a small MCP server for my note-taking app, immediately understood the tradeoffs vs custom tool calls.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Integrity: a time you were honest about a limitation.

rubric.criterion: Cost you might have paid short-term

questions.modelAnswer: S: Interviewing for a project that needed deep AWS IAM expertise; I had shipped IAM basics but never done cross-account trust policies at scale. T: Decide whether to overstate. A: Told the client upfront: 'I've done IAM for single-account; cross-account with STS I'll need a week to ramp. Willing to do it if the timeline supports.' R: Almost lost the project — client considered another candidate. But they picked me because they trusted the assessment. Ramp took 4 days; project shipped on time.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Integrity: a time you kept a commitment when it would have been easy to slip.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Promised a customer a written incident post-mortem within 48 hours. Day 2 I got pulled into another P0. T: Keep the commitment. A: Blocked 90 min at 10pm, wrote the post-mortem myself instead of asking someone else to (my incident, my write-up). Sent it 46 hours after the incident. R: Customer specifically referenced 'you did what you said' at renewal conversation 3 months later.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Collaboration: how do you make async work across time zones?

rubric.criterion: Shipped outcome that would fail without good async

questions.modelAnswer: S: Four engineers, three timezones, no shared meeting time > 2h/day. T: Tech lead. A: Every task had written design doc reviewed async. Daily standup was a written thread. Decisions logged in one doc with author + date. Overlapped 1h with each timezone daily for pair debugging. R: Shipped 6-week project on time with zero re-work from misalignment. Async-by-default is faster than sync-by-default once the team accepts writing over meetings.

questions.prompt: Andela EPIC-Collaboration: a time you helped a teammate succeed.

rubric.criterion: What you did, not just 'I helped'

questions.modelAnswer: S: Junior engineer on my team was struggling with a debugging problem; had been on it 3 days. T: Not my ticket but wanted to unblock. A: Instead of solving it for them, I paired for 30 min showing my debug methodology: reproduce first, then bisect, then check assumptions. They finished it that afternoon. R: Next similar bug, they solved solo in 2 hours. Also: I now do that pattern in onboarding for every new hire.

questions.prompt: Draft a weekly written status update to your executive sponsor. Structure it.

rubric.criterion: Blockers include the ask you need from the reader

questions.modelAnswer:
```
Subject: [Project] weekly — Sept 4

## Shipped this week
- Auth integration end-to-end (SAML from Okta live in staging)
- 2 bug fixes in retrieval pipeline (P95 latency 180ms → 120ms)

## Shipping next week
- Prod rollout of auth (Wed pending your sign-off — see Blockers)
- Add SCIM endpoint for user lifecycle

## Blockers / asks
```

questions.prompt: Draft the Slack DM to your manager: 'the deadline I promised is slipping 5 days.'

rubric.criterion: Leads with the news, not the excuse

questions.modelAnswer:
```
Hey — I need to move the [feature] deadline from Fri Sept 8 to Wed Sept 13.

Root cause: the integration test setup took longer than I estimated (needed to spin up a real Snowflake instance, which I hadn't accounted for). Fully my miss.

Two options if the Sept 8 date is fixed:
(a) Ship without the deploy pipeline; I'd do manual deploy on the 8th, add pipeline the following week
(b) Cut the analytics dashboard scope; ship it in a follow-up

My default is (b). Let me know either way — happy to jump on a call if easier.
```

questions.prompt: Write an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) template — sections + purpose.
questions.modelAnswer:
```
# ADR-013: Use pgvector over Pinecone for vector storage

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-04
**Reviewers:** @alice @bob @charlie

## Context
We need vector similarity search over ~5M product descriptions. Query latency target: <100ms P95.

## Decision
Use pgvector on our existing Postgres. Not Pinecone.

## Alternatives considered
1. Pinecone hosted — simplest, but adds a vendor + $2k/mo
2. Qdrant self-hosted — capable, but adds a service to operate
3. pgvector — leverages existing Postgres + can JOIN with product table

## Rationale
- 5M vectors is well within pgvector HNSW's sweet spot
- Ability to JOIN with relational data is a real workflow (top-K similar in stock)
- Avoids new vendor onboarding

## Consequences
**+** No new service to operate
**+** Cheaper (~$400/mo vs $2k)
**-** If we hit >20M vectors, will need to migrate — expected timeline 18 months out
**-** Requires Postgres 15+ (we're on 14; upgrade planned Q4)
```

questions.prompt: Draft a decision-oriented meeting agenda for a 30-min call with the client.

rubric.criterion: States THE ONE decision to be made

questions.modelAnswer:
```
Subject: 30-min decision call — Sept 6, 2pm ET

**Decision:** Whether to enable SSO in v1 or ship v1 without and add SSO in v1.1.
**Decision-maker:** [Client CTO]

**Pre-read** (5 min): [doc link] — 2 options + tradeoff table.

**Agenda**
- 0:00-0:05 Recap: where we are, what's blocking
- 0:05-0:15 Walk through option A (SSO in v1)
- 0:15-0:25 Walk through option B (v1 without, SSO in v1.1)
- 0:25-0:30 Decision + owner for next step

**Follow-up:** I'll send written summary within 1 hr with decision + owner for follow-up items.
```

questions.prompt: Time you managed disagreement across a distributed team.

rubric.criterion: Used async-friendly tools (written proposal, not meeting)
Reached decision that both sides committed to

questions.modelAnswer: S: Two engineers in different timezones disagreed on API contract style — one wanted GraphQL, one wanted REST. T: I owned the decision. A: Rather than a meeting neither could attend live, wrote a 1-page comparison doc with 4 criteria (client fit, ops complexity, learning curve, migration cost); posted for async review; both wrote their thoughts in comments; decided REST + score-based rationale published. Both committed. R: Contract shipped, no re-litigation later.

questions.prompt: Time you received hard criticism and grew from it.
questions.modelAnswer: S: Manager told me in a 1:1 that my PR reviews were too nitpicky and slowing team velocity. T: Take the feedback. A: Initial reaction was defensive — I thought I was being thorough. Sat with it. Realized: my comments were mostly style, not correctness. Adopted a rule: only 'must-change' vs 'nice-to-have' framing on comments; approved PRs faster with follow-up tickets for polish. R: Team's PR review time dropped ~40%; no drop in code quality metrics. Also became the reviewer people asked for by name.

questions.prompt: Time you delivered on a vague / ambiguous requirement.

rubric.criterion: How you narrowed it — questions asked

questions.modelAnswer: S: Ticket said 'make the report faster.' No target, no baseline, no priority. T: Ship a meaningful speedup. A: Asked PM 2 questions in Slack: (1) what P95 do users experience today (600ms)? (2) what P95 do they need (200ms per PM)? Then measured, found DB was 400ms of it, added an index — 600ms → 90ms. R: Shipped in a day. PM confirmed users noticed. Wrote up the process; became internal template for 'faster' requests.
